answers: The backend layer owns authentication, authorisation, limits, and persistence. Orchestration should not implement authentication because it is responsible for assembling context and controlling the model loop; keeping authentication in the backend gives security one explicit boundary and contract.

Validate the model output against a schema. If the model returns invalid JSON, schema validation fails, so reject the output and return a safe fallback such as “I cannot verify that answer right now,” while recording the validation failure in the trace.

A cited source ID must be checked against the retrieved chunks so the model cannot invent sources. Only chunk IDs that point to actually retrieved chunks are valid; if none match, the answer is rejected.

Streaming complicates persistence because tokens arrive before the full response, so the backend must assemble and validate the complete answer before persisting the turn. It complicates cancellation because if the client disconnects, the server must cancel downstream work rather than continue paying for an answer nobody receives.

When the order service times out, the assistant can report the known policy, say the live status is temporarily unavailable, and offer a callback. That is better than a generic error because it still gives the user useful, verified information.
Record the trace ID, total latency and per-hop timing, model version, input and output token counts, validation result, and whether the degraded path was used.

concepts.example: A retrieval call has an input query, output chunks, a timeout, and a fallback to a plain answer with a warning.
concepts.plain: An AI app has six layers: interface, backend, orchestration, model access, data, and trust. Each boundary between layers needs explicit rules for input, output, timeout, and failure behaviour.

concepts.example: A chat message gets a trace ID so every log from one request can be found later.
concepts.plain: A chat turn starts with HTTPS, authentication, quota checks, and conversation history. The orchestrator retrieves relevant chunks, builds a prompt, and calls a model through a gateway. Tokens stream back while the backend assembles the full response, validates it, and persists the turn with token counts, latency, model version, and a trace ID. Background work updates analytics, memory, and evaluation samples.
concepts.title: One request, many hand-offs

concepts.plain: Plan for failures instead of hoping they won't happen. Every remote call needs a deadline inside the user-facing latency target. Validate model output against a schema, check that cited sources exist, test fallbacks deliberately, and record which path served each request.

0.04.intro: This lesson is about choosing the software pieces for an AI product without adding unnecessary complexity. A beginner should care because every extra piece costs time and money, and missing basic tracking can block launch.

dict.get('price',0.0) returns 0.0 when the key is missing but does not create a new entry; a membership check would reveal that the key was absent and allow you to handle the missing case explicitly.
A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory, so for a 4 GB file it would consume too much RAM; a generator processes one item at a time.
The frame that shows where the exception was raised (the last frame) usually contains the real cause, because it is the line that executed the faulty operation.
Running a file with python -m adds the package’s directory to sys.path, so imports resolve relative to the package; running a script directly does not include that package directory in sys.path.
You can check the number of rows processed and the number of rows used in the average; if they match the expected count, the average is over the intended rows.

concepts.example: A list of dictionaries like [{'name':'A','price':'0.5'}, {'name':'B','price':'1.2'}]
concepts.plain: Data from AI tools comes as lists of small tables. Each table row is a dictionary with named fields. You must keep the types right and avoid changing the data while you read it.
concepts.title: The data shapes you will meet

concepts.example: Using dict.get('price',0) gives 0 instead of an error if 'price' is missing.
concepts.plain: Use short loops that build a new list or generator. They are fast for small data but can use a lot of memory for big files. Tools like dict.get avoid crashes when a key is missing.
concepts.title: Comprehensions and lazy iteration

concepts.example: The last line of a traceback shows where the error happened, not where it started.

concepts.title: Tracebacks and the run loop

1.01.intro: This lesson shows how to handle data, loop through it, and fix errors in Python. It helps you write clear, reliable code for AI projects. You’ll learn the basics you need to start building and debugging scripts.

answers: It stops Python from accidentally importing loose files in the folder you run from. A test can pass only by importing the installed package, so it matches CI and containers.
CI may fail with ImportError: partially initialized module, while local tests pass because modules were imported in a lucky order. That points to two modules importing each other.

__main__.py should contain the small launcher and guard that let python -m model_catalog work. The callable main() should contain the real startup work, such as loading data and printing, so tests can import it without running that work.
Move the shared helper into its own module, such as formatting.py, and have both modules import that. If needed, pass the helper in as an injected function instead.
Importing should have no side effects, so tests stay fast and do not need data or network access. File reads and API calls belong in main(), where tests can choose not to run them.

An editable install makes Python treat your project as an installed package, so import model_catalog resolves from any directory. It replaces sys.path hacks and makes shell, editor, tests, and CI use the same package.

concepts.example: A test imports model_catalog, not a nearby file called loader.py.
concepts.plain: Put your reusable code in a special folder named src. This stops Python from grabbing random files in whatever folder you happen to be in, so tests must use the properly installed package.
concepts.title: src layout, not script soup

concepts.example: main imports catalog; catalog imports schemas; schemas import nothing from the project.
concepts.plain: Split code by the job it does and the reason it changes. Dependencies should flow one way, from the starter file to business rules to data shapes, never back and forth.
concepts.title: Boundaries follow change

concepts.example: Importing main in a test does not read data/models.json or print anything.
concepts.plain: Make one clear starting function and a tiny launcher for python -m. Importing a file should do nothing active; reading files or calling APIs happens only when you actually start the program.
concepts.title: Entry points and import-time calm

1.02.intro: This lesson shows how to arrange Python files so Python finds your code the same way everywhere. A beginner should care because a messy layout can make code fail in tests or containers even when it works on your laptop.

answers: A list default is created once when the function is defined, so every call shares the same list. Replace it with None and create a new list inside the function.
A pure function's output depends only on its arguments, and it changes no external state. That lets tests pass simple literal values with no setup.

A helper should raise when bad input means it cannot produce its promised return value, rather than returning None or an empty string that looks like a valid answer. The lesson's example is parse_usage(response), which returns a Usage or raises ValueError.
Injecting fetch lets tests pass a fake function that returns a fixed response. Tests can run offline and simulate a timeout without patching module internals.
A boolean flag often creates combinations nobody tests and can make one function do several jobs. The caller should choose a different function instead.

Printing, network calls, file writes, and retries belong at the edge of the batch job. The scoring loop should do pure calculation and return a result with a named error per case, not perform those side effects itself.

concepts.example: parse_usage(response) returns a Usage or raises ValueError.
concepts.plain: A function should tell you what it needs and what it gives back without you reading its insides. Give it one clear job and a clear way to fail.
concepts.title: A function is a contract

concepts.example: def add(item, bucket=None): if bucket is None: bucket = [] bucket.append(item) return bucket
concepts.plain: A default list is made once and shared, so old items can appear later. Use None and make a fresh list inside the function. Keep printing, network calls, and file writes outside pure calculations.
concepts.title: Defaults and side effects

concepts.example: Use *, timeout_s=10.0 so callers write timeout_s=5.
concepts.plain: Build big behavior by calling small functions instead of adding switches. If a flag changes what a function returns, use a separate function. Make optional settings keyword-only so calls stay readable.
concepts.title: Composition over cleverness

1.03.intro: This lesson is about writing small functions with clear inputs and outputs. A beginner should care because small pieces are easier to test and easier to fix when one step fails.

answers: A clean mypy run only checks static shapes. TypedDict and Literal do not validate JSON at runtime, so a response with a wrong type (for example prompt_tokens as the string "12") can still type-check and fail later.

list[dict[str, float]] is a list where each item is a dictionary with string keys and float values. dict[str, list[float]] is a single dictionary whose keys are strings and values are lists of floats.

Use NotRequired when the provider may omit that key. Making it required would misstate the API contract and force every test or payload to invent a value for it; NotRequired lets the shape match reality.

An early return such as if value is None: return lets the checker narrow a union (a value that may be one of several types) to the remaining type. After that check, mypy knows value is not None and can check later uses safely.

Any silently disables checking for everything it touches, so a wrong shape can spread without warnings. In strict mode, a missing annotation is an error you must fix; Any can hide the problem instead.

Annotate module boundaries first: loaders, HTTP calls, and anything that builds a prompt or parses a response. That is where outside data enters, so wrong shapes are caught before they travel through the code.

concepts.example: list[dict[str, float]] and dict[str, list[float]] describe different nested shapes.
concepts.plain: An annotation says what a name may hold at that point; mypy tracks it through assignments and branches. list[dict[str, float]] is a list of dictionaries with string keys and float values, while dict[str, list[float]] is a different shape. If a value may be absent, use X | None and narrow it with an early check before use.
concepts.title: Types describe values, not variables

concepts.example: Use Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls"] for a finish reason field.
concepts.plain: TypedDict describes a dictionary with fixed keys and a type for each key, which fits API payloads better than a wide dict[str, object]. Mark optional keys with NotRequired (or use total=False on a separate class). Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls"] makes a magic string a checked set of allowed values. These are static shapes only; they do not validate a response at runtime.
concepts.title: Model JSON with TypedDict and Literal

concepts.example: Add [tool.mypy] with strict = true and run mypy on the package.
concepts.plain: Start with public functions and data crossing module boundaries; private helpers can wait until stable. Run mypy with strict = true in pyproject.toml, then fix errors by adding a missing annotation, narrowing a union, or correcting the shape. reveal_type(value) prints what the checker inferred.
concepts.title: Gradual typing and the checker loop

1.04.intro: Type hints are annotations that describe what values a name may hold. They let editors and mypy catch wrong shapes before runtime. This lesson focuses on JSON-like API data, where some fields may be missing.

answers: A group of functions should become a class when they share state that must remain valid together and that state requires an invariant to be protected.

Network calls in __init__ cause problems because tests cannot construct the object without hitting the real network, and service startup fails if the network is down. Keep __init__ cheap: just store the settings, don't do work.
Injecting a transport allows you to pass a fake version that returns a 429 error first, then a success response, enabling you to test retry logic without touching the real network.
Inheritance is better than composition only when the child class is usable anywhere the parent is and adds no surprising behavior—genuine substitution. Otherwise, pass collaborators in as parameters.
__repr__ should show identifying information like the host and request count so logs are readable. Never include headers, tokens, keys, or personal data that could leak secrets.
Python's underscore convention fails to make an attribute truly private because it is only a signal to other programmers—the language does not enforce it.

concepts.example: A client stores a base URL and always strips trailing slashes, so every request method can assume the URL is clean.
concepts.plain: A class is worth using when multiple functions share data that must follow a rule. For example, a web address should never have a trailing slash, so the class enforces that rule once at the start and every method can trust it afterward.
concepts.title: State plus invariants

concepts.example: Use _transport for internal details, expose record_usage() as a button, and __repr__ shows 'ModelClient(https://api.example.com, requests=5)'.
concepts.plain: Hide the messy details inside the class using underscore names, and let other code interact through simple buttons—methods that do one job. Keep the setup fast and cheap, and write a readable summary of what the object is.
concepts.title: Encapsulation is a convention

concepts.example: Pass a transport function to the client so tests can use a fake that returns errors, and retries can wrap it without subclassing.
concepts.plain: Instead of creating child classes, pass in the pieces you need as parameters. This lets you swap in a fake version for testing or wrap it with extra behavior without changing the original class.
concepts.title: Composition beats inheritance

1.05.intro: This lesson teaches you when to use classes—a way to bundle related data and behavior together. You'll learn that classes work best when you have information that must stay consistent, like an API client that always needs a valid web address.

answers: A bare list default fails in a dataclass because dataclasses reject the shared-default bug at definition time: the list would be created once and shared by every instance. A normal function allows a mutable default, but it is also evaluated once and shared across calls, so it can cause the same kind of bug; dataclasses catch it early.

Value equality helps for records that represent facts, such as a usage report or a CaseResult, where two instances with the same field values should be treated as the same. It is misleading for client objects that hold unique resources like sockets, where identity matters more than matching field values.

frozen=True blocks attribute assignment after construction and makes instances hashable by field value, so a record can be used as a dictionary key or in a set. It does not make nested mutable objects deeply immutable; for example, a list field can still be mutated.

Post-init checks belong in __post_init__ for invariants the type system cannot express, such as a score being between 0 and 1 or a non-negative token count. These checks make the record valid at construction, so callers do not have to enforce them later.

A dataclass does not coerce types (like turning the string "12" into 12), reject unknown fields, or explain validation errors to an API caller. Use a schema model such as Pydantic at the trust boundary where untrusted JSON arrives, then convert to a dataclass for internal use.
Calling asdict() inside a per-token loop causes measurable allocation because it deep-copies nested records. On a small batch it is fine, but in a hot loop the repeated copying adds up.

concepts.example: Two CaseResult records with the same case_id and score compare as equal without you writing comparison code.
concepts.plain: A dataclass automatically writes the boring setup code for you. You just list the fields, and the dataclass creates the methods that compare records, display them, and initialize them. Two records with identical data are treated as equal.
concepts.title: Generated methods, visible shape

concepts.example: A frozen CaseResult rejects a score of 1.4 immediately in __post_init__ instead of letting bad data slip through.
concepts.plain: A frozen dataclass blocks attribute assignment after creation and makes instances hashable, so it can be used as a dictionary key or in a set. You can add a __post_init__ validation step that runs after creation to check invariants the type system cannot express, such as a score being between 0 and 1.
concepts.title: Frozen records and invariants

concepts.example: Validate JSON from an API with Pydantic first, then convert the result to a frozen dataclass for your pipeline.
concepts.plain: A dataclass trusts the data it receives, but the outside world is messy. Use a schema validator (like Pydantic) at the boundary where untrusted data arrives, then convert to a dataclass for safe internal use.
concepts.title: Dataclass or schema model

1.06.intro: This lesson teaches you how to write simple data containers that organize information without writing repetitive code. You will learn to build records that are safe, clear, and work well in AI pipelines.

answers: A dataclass only describes the shape of the data; it does not enforce it. Pydantic also enforces the shape while constructing the object, so a string where an integer belongs fails right at the boundary instead of surfacing three functions later as a confusing TypeError.

Coercion helps with messy input, such as a sloppy CSV export where the string '128000' should become the number 128000. It hides a defect when a numeric string must fail, such as a price arriving as 'cheap' or a context window as '128k', so use StrictInt or strict=True on those fields.

The loc tuple is the machine-readable path to the failing field, including nested model prefixes, like ('pricing', 'input_usd'). The msg tells you what went wrong but not which field in a nested payload, so loc is what lets you pinpoint and log the exact field.

A cross-field validator runs after the individual fields have passed. If a field fails validation first, there is no valid object to check, so the cross-field validator never runs; fix the field-level errors before debugging business rules.

Wrap each record in try/except ValidationError, log the record index, the error loc, and the error type, then continue with the next row. That way one bad record is quarantined and the rest of the 2,400-row import still completes.

Mark strict the fields that represent money or limits, such as input_usd, output_usd, and context_window. These must be actual numbers, not strings that look like numbers, because a billing or routing system cannot afford silent type confusion.

concepts.example: When a provider sends you an offer, validate that context_window is a number greater than 0 before storing it.
concepts.plain: Create a schema (a template) for each type of data that enters your program, then check the data against that schema as soon as it arrives. Once it passes, the rest of your code can trust it's correct and needs no defensive checks.
concepts.title: Parse at the boundary

concepts.example: A context_window field might require a number greater than 0 and at most 2,000,000; lax mode turns the string '128000' into the number 128000, but '128k' still fails.
concepts.plain: You can set rules on fields, like 'must be greater than 0' or 'at most 2,000,000.' Pydantic's default lax mode also converts compatible values automatically, but you can turn that off with StrictInt or strict=True when a string must fail.
concepts.title: Constraints and coercion

concepts.example: If row 42 has an invalid price, log the row number and the failing field's loc, then move on to row 43.
concepts.plain: When validation fails, you get one ValidationError containing every problem, each with a loc, msg, type, and input. You can use this information to skip bad records and keep processing good ones.
concepts.title: Errors are structured data

1.07.intro: This lesson teaches you how to check that data coming into your program is correct before you use it. When your code receives information from providers, LLM output, or a database, it can be missing, misnamed, or the wrong type—Pydantic catches those problems at the boundary so the rest of your code works with typed objects instead of breaking later.

answers: KeyError usually means your code asked for a field or key that is not there, such as a record with no body field. That is a programming bug, not a normal production condition, so it should crash in development instead of being swallowed at a loop boundary.
Never retry 400, 401, 403, or 422. They will fail identically on the second attempt, waste quota, and delay surfacing the real error.

raise NewError(...) from exc preserves the original exception as __cause__, so the traceback shows both the translation boundary and the underlying cause. An on-call engineer sees the full story instead of only the new error.

A write is safe to retry only when it has an idempotency key, which lets the server recognize a repeated write and return the first result instead of creating a duplicate. Without it, a retried POST can create two orders.

If an outer job and an inner client both retry, the attempts multiply; the lesson’s example is that four attempts can become sixteen. Put the retry policy in one layer and pass the remaining deadline down.

A skip count or error-rate metric would have exposed Nadia’s silent data loss: 1,340 tickets were absent even though the run reported success. Alerting on skip count/rate, not only process exit, would have caught it.

concepts.example: Catch FileNotFoundError to use a default, but let KeyError crash because it means your code has a bug.
concepts.plain: Catch only the specific errors you know how to handle. Let bugs crash so you notice them, but catch real failures like missing files or network timeouts and do something about them.
concepts.title: Catch what you can act on

concepts.example: Retry a 503 server error, but never retry a 401 permission denied—it will fail identically and waste your quota.
concepts.plain: Some failures are temporary and will work if you try again; others will always fail the same way. Retry timeouts and server errors, but never retry permission errors or bad requests.
concepts.title: Retry only what can succeed twice

concepts.example: Store failed records in a dead-letter queue with their error type and timestamp so you can inspect and replay them after fixing the bug.
concepts.plain: Keep a record of every failure that exhausted all retries, with the data and error type, so you can fix it later and replay it. Never silently skip records.
concepts.title: Make every failure observable

1.08.intro: When code fails in production, you need to know why and what to do about it. This lesson teaches you to catch only the failures you can fix, retry the right ones, and make sure nothing disappears silently.

answers: A 200 means the transport succeeded, not that the payload is usable. You still must check Content-Type, decode the JSON, and validate its shape against a schema before your application trusts it.

The client should retry only transient status codes such as 429, 502, 503, and 504, and it should honor Retry-After when present. Transport timeouts belong to one job-level wrapper so retries do not multiply.
Reusing one client skips repeated DNS, TCP, and TLS setup. Set pool limits, such as 50 total connections and 20 keep-alive connections, to bound concurrency and match worker concurrency.
Automatic redirects can send an authenticated request to a different host. A 302 could forward your bearer token, so disable redirects for authenticated calls.
Retry-After tells you when to try again instead of using your normal backoff. It can be a number of seconds or an HTTP date, and production code must parse both forms.
Record status, latency, retry count, provider request id, and token usage for each call. Compare 5xx rate and p95, and include a request id to trace failures.

concepts.example: Ask for a translation with POST; a 200 may still contain malformed or unexpected JSON that breaks parsing.
concepts.plain: A request carries a method, URL, headers, and an optional body; a response carries a status, headers, and a body. A 2xx success code only means the transport succeeded. You still inspect and validate the content before trusting it.
concepts.title: A request is a typed message

concepts.example: If the server says retry after 2 seconds, wait 2 seconds instead of guessing.
concepts.plain: Set a total deadline for the whole call, and shorten it on each retry. Retry only temporary failures, wait when told, and stop after a few tries.
concepts.title: Deadlines and retries

concepts.example: Reuse one client for many calls; validate the decoded JSON with Pydantic before use.
concepts.plain: Keep one client open and reuse it so setup work is not repeated. Turn off redirects for authenticated calls and check every reply against an expected shape.
concepts.title: Reuse connections and verify responses

1.10.intro: This lesson explains how a program calls another service over the internet. It covers time limits, safe retries, reusing connections, and checking that the response is usable.

answers: Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. If you call it and discard it, you may only see RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited at garbage collection, and you can accidentally serialize the coroutine object instead of its result.

Sequential awaits do not overlap because the next call or awaitable is created/started only after the previous await returns. The total latency is the sum: two 5-second calls awaited one after another take about 10 seconds. Use asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup when the calls are independent.

TaskGroup is structured: if one child fails, the other children are cancelled and the error surfaces as an ExceptionGroup when the scope exits, so no child outlives the block. gather with return_exceptions=True does not fail-fast-cancel siblings; it lets tasks finish and returns each result or exception in the result list.

CancelledError means the task is being cancelled, often because the client disconnected or a timeout fired. If you catch it, do cleanup and re-raise it so the caller knows the work stopped; converting it to a 500 can send a stale payload to a client that already left and can hide the cancellation.

asyncio.shield is justified only when an awaitable must keep running even if its parent task is cancelled. The risk is an orphaned task that keeps running after the request stops, may waste resources, and may lose its exceptions unless it is tracked, awaited, or cancelled at shutdown.

An async context manager uses async with to run cleanup during unwinding, including cancellation. Its __aexit__ method closes the connection before CancelledError propagates further; keep that cleanup non-blocking.

concepts.example: Two API calls awaited one after another take 10 seconds total, not 5, because the second call does not start until the first returns.
concepts.plain: When you await, your code pauses and lets other work happen. Think of it like pausing a video to let someone else watch theirs, then resuming when it's your turn again.
concepts.title: await is a suspension point

concepts.example: If one database lookup fails inside a TaskGroup, the other lookup is cancelled at the next await point.
concepts.plain: A TaskGroup is a scope that waits for all its child tasks to finish. If one child fails, the others are cancelled and you get a grouped error when the scope exits rather than leaving tasks running in the background.
concepts.title: Tasks own lifetimes

concepts.example: async with client.stream() guarantees the connection closes even if the user disconnects mid-response.
concepts.plain: An async context manager opens and closes resources safely, even if the body raises or is cancelled. Async iterators let you process streamed data one chunk at a time, which helps with time-to-first-token and stopping early.
concepts.title: Async context and iteration

1.15.intro: This lesson teaches precise async/await: what await actually does, how errors and cancellation travel, and how to avoid orphaned tasks. You'll learn why a missing await can silently return a coroutine object and how to stop tasks cleanly when clients disconnect.

Unit tests cover pure transforms such as prompt assembly, response parsing, retry classification, and cost calculation. Nightly contract tests check your client still matches the provider's real request and response shapes.
Injecting sleep keeps the test instant while still exercising the backoff decision. A real sleep would add one or two seconds and slow the suite.
A parametrised test reports each input case separately, often with readable ids. A loop inside one test reports only one pass or fail for the whole loop.
A flaky test fails for reasons unrelated to your code, and rerunning until green erodes trust in the gate. It can train the team to ignore real failures.
Assert that a 429 is retried, the retry count and backoff are correct, and it is not treated as terminal. Only 429 and 5xx should be retried.

concepts.example: Fake a 429 response and check your code retries.
concepts.plain: Test the parts you control, like building requests and handling errors, using fake responses. Save rare real checks for provider changes, and keep model quality separate.
concepts.title: Test the seams, not the model

concepts.example: Run one test for 400, 429, 500, timeout, and bad JSON.
concepts.plain: Fixtures are reusable setup helpers passed into tests by name. Parametrisation runs one test over many inputs so each case reports separately.
concepts.title: Fixtures and parametrisation

concepts.example: Use a fake HTTP handler to return 500 and check the retry.
concepts.plain: Replace the network layer, not your own code, so your real client still builds and parses requests. This catches broken requests and retry mistakes.
concepts.title: Mock at the transport

1.16.intro: This lesson is about checking that your program behaves correctly without waiting for or paying for a real AI service. You will learn to use fake responses so tests are fast, repeatable, and trustworthy.
